resources.string: Adult anatomy. The cutaway and nerve diagrams show structure and the direction of normal sensory signals, not to scale.
The midline clitoral body ends in the glans. The two crura extend from the body along the pubic arch. The vestibular bulbs lie medial to the crura and are distinct structures.
Branches of sensory fibers end within tissue of the glans. A single signal is shown traveling from one peripheral ending toward the parent nerve.
On either side, the dorsal nerve of the clitoris carries sensory signals from the glans and body toward the pudendal nerve. The diagram follows one side.
Sensory fibers in the pudendal nerve return via sacral spinal nerves. A signal enters the spinal cord through a dorsal root. One route is shown.
The paired cavernous bodies form the central body, which continues distally to the glans.
The glans is the rounded distal part of the clitoris. It contains sensory nerve endings.
Each crus continues from one of the two cavernous bodies and follows its side of the pubic arch.
The bulbs are a separate pair of erectile tissues on either side of the vestibule, medial to the crura.

Adult anatomy. Schematics show gland position, microscopic structure, and the direction of normal mucus movement, not to scale.
Two small glands sit deep on either side of the posterior vaginal opening. Their ducts open onto the vestibule at the posterolateral margins, separate from the urethral opening farther forward.
Each gland contains clusters of small secretory units called acini. Mucus-producing epithelial cells line the acini and release mucus into their central spaces.
Small branches collect mucus from the acini into one main duct per gland. The moving traces show the direction of mucus within the duct spaces.
Mucus passes out of each short main duct onto the vestibular surface beside the vaginal opening. Neither duct opens into the urethra or the vagina.
This separate opening is anterior to the vaginal opening and the two gland duct outlets.
The two greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands sit deep in the tissue. Each contains many small mucus-secreting acini.
Each gland has its own slender main duct that carries mucus to the vestibular surface.
The outlets are posterolateral to the vaginal opening, approximately at 4 and 8 o’clock in this orientation.
